content_metadata.description: Presentation by Jesslyn Tannady on XR and neural-computer interfaces, focusing on ControlKit as a solution to current XR input limitations.

qAndA.answer: Electromyography (EMG), which measures electrical signals produced by muscle activity.
qAndA.question: What is the primary technology used by ControlKit to capture the user’s intentions?

qAndA.answer: EMG eliminates occlusion issues (hands being hidden from the camera) and latency problems associated with computer vision-based solutions.
qAndA.question: What is the advantage of using EMG over computer vision for hand tracking in VR?

qAndA.answer: Productivity tools, robotics control, clinical applications, and art installations.
qAndA.question: Besides gaming and VR, what other applications does Jesslyn suggest ControlKit could be used for?

qAndA.answer: It shows the potential of ControlKit for assistive technology, enabling individuals with physical limitations to interact with virtual environments and control devices in new ways.
qAndA.question: What is the significance of the demonstration with the scientific advisor who has a partially developed hand?

qAndA.answer: 'Force Control' allows users to control the speed and intensity of object movement by varying their muscle tension, providing a more nuanced and intuitive way to interact with virtual objects compared to pressing buttons on a controller.
qAndA.question: How does the demonstration of 'Force Control' differ from traditional VR interaction methods?

activities.description: Jesslyn introduces herself and the topic of her talk: XR and neural-computer interfaces.
Jesslyn expresses her dissatisfaction with current XR input devices, citing their limited functionality, the awkwardness of holding controllers, and the inconvenience of typing in VR.

She emphasizes the need for a better way to interact with virtual environments and introduces Control Labs, a company focusing on eliminating the barrier between machines and the human nervous system.

characterInteraction.description: Jesslyn is the only character in this scene.

scenes.contextualRelevance: The frustration Jesslyn expresses resonates with XR developers and users who have experienced the limitations of current input devices, creating a shared understanding of the need for a new approach.

mood.description: Curious. The presentation starts with a sense of curiosity, transitioning from a playful and inviting logo animation to Jesslyn's introduction, raising the question of the future of XR. The visual style is clean and professional, with a focus on text-based slides and a few illustrative images.

activities.description: Jesslyn explains that humans process information at a high bandwidth, but current interfaces are low bandwidth.
She introduces ControlKit, a device worn on the arm that allows users to interact with virtual environments using hand movements and subtle muscle tension, detected by EMG sensors.

Jesslyn showcases ControlKit's capabilities in VR, highlighting the ability to bring hands into virtual environments and interact naturally, eliminating the need for controllers. A video demonstrates how a user’s hand movements are mirrored by a virtual hand.
Jesslyn discusses the ability to map letters to muscle tension to allow for typing in VR without a physical keyboard. A video shows a user typing on a virtual keyboard by flexing their muscles.

She explains the potential for using subtle muscle tensions to control objects at a distance, demonstrating “Force Control” using a video where a user controls a block’s movement towards them with their muscle tension.
She emphasizes the concept of “Intention Capture,” showing a video where the device recognizes a user’s intention to open their hand even though they do not physically open it.

Jesslyn introduces “Adaptive Control,” explaining that the device can learn different neuron fire patterns and map them to various actions, including controlling limbs that don’t exist. She showcases a video of a co-worker with a partially developed hand using ControlKit to manipulate a virtual hand with a full set of fingers, demonstrating its potential for assistive technology.
Jesslyn encourages the audience to join the ControlKit waitlist and to explore its possibilities.
She expresses her excitement for the future of neural interfaces and concludes her presentation.

timecoded_text_to_speech.text: Thanks for coming out here today. My name is Jusslin and I'm a technical product manager
at Control Labs. Now a huge reason I'm here at Control Labs is because as an XR developer
and as a human being, I felt that down by a lot of the commercial XR input devices available
out there today. I spend enough time in this medium to believe in its expansive potential,
but I feel like if we want to give XR a meaningful chance at a successful future, we need to
really re-examine our interactive toolkit. And I'm sure many of you guys share my frustration
with current things in XR. For example, I feel like we're limited by our controllers.
Have you ever noticed that a lot of commercial XR controllers are kind of remote-shaped?
So you can't really do something like pick up something big and round like a basketball
because let's say you wanted to do that with an Oculus Touch controller, you'd reach
out, press a trigger with your index button, and then if you wanted to grow this basketball,
you would grow your hand up, but release the index button. But it doesn't feel intuitive
and the entire time you're holding something that's raw-d shaped and that just feels weird.
Or do you ever think about how ergonomically absurd it is that we have to hold our hand
out in front of our face every time we want to do something meaningful in XR,
there's just a lot of arm fatigue there. And also, what type of typing in XR have you
ever had to type your password in using HoloLens and it's like, quick, quick, quick, and it's
so slow and it's so frustrating. So there has to be a better way.
We have a massive opportunity to rewrite interaction paradigms about how we interact
with virtual environments. And a lot of my frustrations, the way things are in XR today
is what brought me to Control Labs. Control Labs is an interdisciplinary team of scientists,
engineers, and designers. And we're focused on eliminating the barrier between machines
and human nervous system. We imagine a world where computers are natural extensions of
thought and movement. Because our brains and our thoughts are so high bandwidth, we process
a remarkable amount of sensory information every single second. And yet, the way we interface
with the world is so go bandwidth, whether we're interacting with the physical world, using
our limbs to touch things or interacting with the virtual world, using our limbs to control
our mouse, keyboard, Xbox controller, and using that as digital input. Even things like
eye tracking and voice commands are so many words I can get out of my mouth at any given
time. Simply put, it's just not, it just doesn't capture the richness and potential of what
we have to work with. And it's super go bandwidth and there's a lot being lost here. So we
wanted to create a universal controller because what if we weren't limited by our devices
or by our bodies, but instead by what our nervous system could do? And that's why we created
a control kit. Control kit is a device that sits on your arm, a little bit like a watch.
And we focus on the hand because it's the most densely innovative part of the human body.
The electrodes read your EMG signals from your skin and we feed that information through
machine learning algorithms to extract signal from that noise. Now as a developer, you plug
that into your applications or your projects and suddenly you have a whole host of new data
to work with right at your fingertips. And a cool thing about this is that it's non-invasive
so there's no suits, no gloves. It's untethered so you don't have to be attached to your
big computer. And in fact, you don't even need a big expensive computer to do this. And
since we don't use cameras, you don't have to deal with occlusion, right? And you don't
have to deal with all that kind of latency that's associated with computer vision based
solutions. And unlike most brain machine interfaces, you don't have to go to surgery and kind
of implant something to your brain to make this work. But more importantly, you don't
have to worry this big cap with wires coming out of it because it's be real who wants
to worry that in public, right? So now that we have this, what can you do with this?
Well, what if you could bring your hands into virtual environments and faithfully interact
with the virtual world the way you'd interact with the real world? So this is kind of an
old video so the device looks a little bit different today. But what you're noticing is
that he doesn't have this in my coworker, he doesn't have to hold anything. So he's
not limited by the shape of the controller or the positioning of buttons. He's no longer
limited by the controller, so he's no longer playing the controller. He can for the first
time play the actual game. So we freed ourselves from having to conform to a controller. And
that opens up all different types of experiences that we can finally build. To go back to the basketball
example, it's now fun or like, it's now possible to be able to hold something in a virtual
environment that's shaped like a basketball that's not rod shape. And because we're not
using cameras, there's no reason why your hand has to stay in front of your face. They

this soft grasp and this hard grasp go exactly the same. But to EMG sensors, they can pick
up the different neurons, neuron pattern fires, and these go wildly different. And what's
cool about this is that it's able to finally differentiate between varying levels of muscle
tension. So suddenly you get a whole dimension of continuous control that you couldn't possibly
get with computer vision-based solutions. Imagine manipulating an art piece, an interactive
art piece without having to move. Cool. So let's take this one step further. What if you

we've effectively created here is intention capture. Now the next thing I want to talk about
is what we call adaptive control. And I think this is one of the coolest things that control
kit gives you. So control kit reads your neuron fires, right? Instead of like what your body
or what your hand is actually doing. So with adaptive control, this thing could earn you.
So let's say I wanted a program at D-pad. I could program it to, let's say my wrist
angle like up, down, left, right. I could map it to say to my fingers, so up, down, left,
right. Or I could just do this. And this is up, down, left, right. I'm like flexing my muscles
a little bit differently and firing and isolating different neurons. And it's able to work
at that control mapping. So whatever control mapping, whether continuous, discrete, big,
and obvious or subtle, it reads all that and it earns that. So what does this mean? Well,
what if you truly didn't have to make any big movements to control things? So I think
this is kind of a cute video. But what we have here is someone being able to play the
Dino runner game without having to move it all. And his hand doesn't even have to be there.
He could just cross his arms and just put his hands wherever he wants and he's able
to isolate the neuron and trigger it and control this Dino rider game. Now if this goes
to your neuron fire patterns, you could map neuron fire patterns to anything. Say to
control limbs that you don't even have. So we gave this device to one of our scientific
advisors and like you or me, he was able to control, you know, like the virtual hand away
any normal person would. But the difference here is that he never actually had a fully
developed left hand. And yet he's able to finally control all these fingers and all these
limbs that he never even had. Imagine being able to finally build experiences that
transcend what our limbs are capable of. And you see here that he's also able to control
grass even though he physically cannot grasp and he's able to like finally control the
level of grass. So all of this is done without a camera over dynamic range, predictably,
reliably. And this is a huge game changer not only for XR but for how we fundamentally
interact with our machines, games, robots, cars, art installations, whatever. And this
feels like the future to me. So what's next? Well, we're currently taking applications
for our independent developer program. So if you're someone who has an appetite for
